errors.english: the Buddhist does not accept that the death of trees caused by stripping all their bark is a valid proof
errors.why: The Tibetan says that the trees' dying when stripped is not established for the Buddhist (the reason is unestablished); 'is a valid proof' is not in the text and shifts the point from the reason's non-establishment to its probative force.

note: A sound rendering of Vinītadeva's treatment of asiddha with the Digambara example; only a small slant in how the non-establishment for the Buddhist is phrased.

errors.english:
A person who desires happiness elsewhere 
Should not be despised in this world,
And should perform whatever leads 
To happiness in the next life as well.
errors.why: The verse says the person who wants happiness hereafter should do what is not censured in this world and brings happiness in the next; 'not censured' qualifies the action, not the person.

fix.find:
Should not be despised in this world,
And should perform whatever leads 
To happiness in the next life as well.
fix.replace:
Should do whatever is not censured in this world
And leads to happiness 
In the next life as well.

errors.english: should abandon pride and act like a spiritual teacher or a lord toward others
errors.why: The sentence continues on the next side with 'should not despise others', i.e. having given up pride one should not look down on others as a superior or a master would; the English makes acting like a superior the recommendation.

fix.find: should abandon pride and act like a spiritual teacher or a lord toward others
fix.replace: should abandon pride and not, like a superior or a master, [look down on others]

note: The narrative (buffalo sacrifice, butcher's son) is well rendered, but one verse is misconstrued and the final sentence is completed with the opposite sense.

errors.english: it is pervaded by one portion of the direction of the property of the (subject) dharmin that is to be proven
errors.why: ཕྱོགས here is pakṣa (the thesis), not a direction: the property of the subject to be proven is pervaded by a part of the pakṣa.

fix.find: it is pervaded by one portion of the direction of the property of the (subject) dharmin that is to be proven
fix.replace: the property of the (subject) dharmin to be proven is pervaded by one part of the thesis (pakṣa)

errors.english: the term "pervasion" Sanskrit: vyāpti is mentioned
errors.why: The word glossed is the participle of the definition (pakṣadharmas tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ), 'pervaded' (vyāpta), as the following gloss on the pervaded being pervaded by the pervader shows, not the abstract vyāpti.

errors.english: In order to understand the pervader, it is appropriate to understand the qualified itself.
errors.why: The Tibetan says the qualified (pervaded) is fit to be the means of making known (gamaka) with respect to the pervader as what is to be made known (gamya); the gamaka/gamya relation is lost.

note: The argument can be followed, but key logical terms (pakṣa, vyāpta, gamaka/gamya) are blurred in places, which a specialist would need to repair.

errors.english: He was like the Master of the Immortals [note: Indra] or the Teacher of the Gods [note: Brihaspati].
errors.why: The phrase most likely names one figure, the divine guru of the Lord of the Immortals (Bṛhaspati, Indra's preceptor), to whom the learned king is compared, not Indra and Bṛhaspati as two comparisons.

note: The verses closing the Ṛṣi-jātaka and the opening of the next story are rendered faithfully overall, with only one doubtful construal of an epithet.

errors.why: In this logical context འཁྲུལ་པ is the deviation (vyabhicāra) of the reason, not delusion: the inconclusiveness is the same.

fix.replace: Because the deviation (vyabhicāra) is the same.

errors.english: Even if any particularity of wind and so forth is the cause, all particularities will not be endowed with all attachments and so forth; because at all times a definite result is seen, it is to be inferred.
errors.why: Everything from གལ་ཏེ to ཞེས་དོགས་པ་བསུ་བ is the objection anticipated by 'However, the result...'; the English presents its first part as the author's own statement.

errors.english: therefore fire itself is the cause of smoke, but the direction is not
errors.why: ཕྱོགས here is the place or locus (cf. ས་ཕྱོགས on the next side): fire, not the place, is the cause of smoke.

note: A very literal word-for-word rendering of dense commentary that is often hard to follow, with a mistranslated logical term and an objection not marked off as such.

errors.english: Who were they? They were those of very youthful form.
errors.why: The gloss identifies what she looked on as food: her cubs, of very young form; 'cubs' (ཕྲུ་གུ) is dropped, which obscures the referent.

note: A careful lemma-by-lemma rendering of the commentary on the tigress episode; only a minor loss of referent.

errors.english: When one does not leave the walking area
errors.why: The side opens by completing the previous sentence: apart from [grass in which creatures] do not breed, the rest should be thrown away; this ruling is not translated.

note: The Vinaya rules and the opening of the Udāyin narrative for the eviction pāyantika are rendered accurately, apart from the untranslated opening clause.

errors.english: Now, if you say that the very mention of "proving the probandum" [note: the thing to be proven] is not what makes it specific, it is indeed not made specific.
errors.why: The opponent proposes that mentioning 'proving the probandum' is itself the needed qualification (rhetorical 'is it not…?'), and the reply denies it; the English has the opponent deny it and the author agree.

note: A generally accurate rendering of the debate about qualifying the statement of similarity, verses correctly set off; one objection-and-reply is muddled.

errors.english: introduces the (Samkhya) an ancient school of Hindu philosophy position; namely, color and so forth
errors.why: In context 'etc.' brings in further enumerated qualities (number/what is counted, alongside color), not the Sāṃkhya school, as 'namely, color and so forth' shows.

errors.english: If one wonders how there is no (concordance) invariable presence in similar cases
errors.why: Here རྗེས་སུ་འགྲོ་བ is the universal's running through its instances (anugama), not logical anvaya 'presence in similar cases'.

note: A faithful lemma-by-lemma rendering of the cowness/universal argument, with two misleading glosses.

errors.english: That [note: absolute reality] is not of the same class as this [note: deluded appearance]. By whom is it seen?
errors.why: རིགས here means 'fit/accessible', not 'class': suchness is not accessible, and the question is 'to whom?', answered by 'all who are not seers of the highest'.

fix.find: That [note: absolute reality] is not of the same class as this [note: deluded appearance]. By whom is it seen?
fix.replace: Suchness (tattva) is not accessible. To whom?

errors.english: regarding that very meaning which is characterized by equanimity—meaning the suchness that is free from defined characteristics and remains in equanimity—the Buddhas
errors.why: It is the Buddhas who are indifferent (upekṣaka) toward the reality-object free of characteristics; the English makes equanimity a property of suchness.

fix.find: regarding that very meaning which is characterized by equanimity—meaning the suchness that is free from defined characteristics and remains in equanimity—the Buddhas
fix.replace: indifferent to the object that is reality—that is, treating with indifference the object of suchness, free from characteristics—the Buddhas

errors.english: [note: a steady, direct, and all-encompassing look]
errors.why: The 'elephant's look' (gajanimīlikā) is the elephant's feigned non-seeing, as the text itself explains: having seen reality, they act as if not seeing it.

fix.find: [note: a steady, direct, and all-encompassing look]
fix.replace: [note: gajanimīlikā, the elephant's half-closed look, seeing while appearing not to see]

errors.english: If suchness is not logical for those who are not seers of the ultimate, why mention "the grasped" and so forth?
errors.why: The commentator asks why suchness is not accessible to non-seers of the highest, and the root words 'the grasped…' give the answer; the English turns this into a question about why those words are mentioned and renders རིགས་པ as 'logical'.

note: The overall movement of the Yogācāra passage is preserved, but the key verse words (tattva not accessible, the Buddhas' indifference, the elephant's look) are misconstrued.
